activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games, an effect called home advantage.
story:
The couch was full by the time the second quarter started, so Blake sat on the floor with his plate of pizza balanced on his knees. Jeremiah had claimed the beanbag, Samir was squished between Blake's dad and Ms. Hu, the neighbour from across the hall who had brought over a bowl of grapes because, she said, "Every game needs fruit." The Wolves were up by six, and when their point guard stole the ball and dunked it, the whole living room erupted.

"That's four in a row," Blake's dad said, holding up four fingers. "Unbeatable at home."

"They're not unbeatable anywhere," Jeremiah argued, tossing a grape in the air and catching it in his mouth. "They just had an easy week. They played the Rustlers twice, and the Rustlers are basically a fungus growing on the bottom of the standings."

Samir laughed, but Blake was chewing on something besides the pizza. "Wait. Four in a row at home. But on the road trip last month they lost three straight." He wiped his hands on a napkin. "I want to actually check this. Everybody just says stuff."

The room groaned in a friendly way, but nobody told him to stop. Ms. Hu scooted over so Blake could reach the laptop on the side table, and he allocated the rest of the halftime break to his project: no snack refill, no highlights commentary, just standings. He copied home records and away records for every team in the league into his notebook, column by column, while Samir called out numbers and Jeremiah double-checked them against the screen.

"Okay," Blake said when the third quarter buzzer sounded. "Almost every team has a better record at home. Not all of them, but most. And when I add it all up, home teams win more than half their games across the whole league."

"There's a name for that," Ms. Hu said from the couch. "Home advantage."

"Right, thanks." Blake circled his total. "So the Wolves winning four straight at home isn't just an easy week, Jeremiah. It fits the pattern. But it's not a magic spell either, because the pattern says more than half, not all."

Jeremiah studied the notebook, chewing his lip. "So if they win tonight, we can't say it's only because they're at home."

"Exactly. It's a real thing, but it's not the whole thing," Blake said. Samir grinned and flipped the notebook around so Blake's dad could see the columns, and even the announcer seemed to agree, because the halftime stat popped up on the screen right then: league home winning percentage, exactly the shape of Blake's numbers.

"With three minutes left, the Wolves were up two, then one, then tied, and the whole couch was leaning forward like one creature. When the final shot rattled in, Blake's dad threw his arms around Ms. Hu, Samir pounded Blake's shoulder, and Jeremiah shouted over the noise, "Show me that notebook again, I want to add this game to it."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: A warm-up of light jogging and moving stretches raises heart rate and muscle temperature, which helps muscles work better before a hard effort.
story:
Evan had watched the tryout list go up on Monday, and by Thursday he had convinced himself of one thing: everyone trying out for the basketball team was faster than he was. He stood at the edge of the gym with Rhys, both of them in shorts despite the October chill outside, while Coach blew the whistle for warm-up laps.

"I'm not wasting energy," Rhys said, planting himself against the padded wall. "I want to see how the eighth graders move before it's my turn. Perspective, you know? Scout the competition."

Evan started to join him, then hesitated. He thought about Saturday, when he had helped his dad carry boxes up three flights of stairs. He'd stood around first, feeling stiff, and the first box had felt terrible; by the fifth trip his legs had loosened up and it was almost easy. Something about starting slow before working hard had made the difference, and he wondered if the same thing might apply here.

"Five minutes of scouting isn't going to teach you their plays," Evan said, and jogged off to do the laps with the others. He moved through the stretches that Coach called out, lunges and leg swings and arm circles, until his t-shirt stuck to his back and his heart was thumping hard in his chest. His legs felt springy, almost impatient.

The eighth graders ran their drills first, and they were fast. But when the whistle blew for the seventh graders, Evan noticed something odd: the two boys who had been sitting on the bench for the entire warm-up, arms crossed, watching everyone else, were the ones stumbling. One of them grabbed his hamstring halfway down the court and hobbled off grimacing, muttering something that made the coach intervene and send him to the water fountain to walk it off. The other, a tall kid Evan vaguely knew from math, kept shaking out his legs like they belonged to someone else.

Evan flew down the court. He couldn't see why his legs felt so good, exactly, but the pattern was there, plain as anything: the kids who jogged and stretched before the drills looked quick and loose, and the kids who skipped it looked like rusty robots. He decided to test it once more at the shooting station, keeping his feet moving in the line instead of standing still. When his turn came he sank four of five.

Rhys, meanwhile, went up for his layup like a man made of cinderblocks and missed the rim entirely. "Your scouting report didn't cover the part where your own legs betray you," Evan said as they switched stations.

"That's it. Next tryout, I'm warming up so hard I need a warm-up for my warm-up." Rhys shook out his arms, and his next shot actually hit the backboard, which he celebrated like a championship.

When the coach posted the callback list, Evan's name was on it, third from the top. Rhys wasn't, but beside the list was a sign-up sheet for a second open tryout in two weeks. Rhys grabbed the pen before anyone else could touch it.

"Start me a lap," he said. "I'll catch up."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: During a severe drought on Daphne Major in 1977, small seeds ran out, and medium ground finches with larger, deeper beaks survived better because they could crack large, hard seeds.
story:
The finch skeleton on Ms. Wijaya's desk had a beak like a pair of pliers, and Ellie had to explain it to the whole class on Friday. She despised presentations. Her voice always went up at the end, like every sentence was asking permission. But the assignment was the assignment, and she'd been diligent about the research, which was the problem: she had forty facts and no story, and Ms. Wijaya had said, "Tell us why, Ellie. Anyone can tell us what."

She was still stuck on Thursday, sitting on the bleachers behind the gym with Deacon and Jake, splitting a bag of sunflower seeds. Jake cracked his with his teeth, fast, one after another. Deacon picked through the bag, frowning. "All the small ones are gone," he said. "You ate the easy ones first."

Ellie looked at the two seeds left in Deacon's palm. Both big, both stubborn. Jake leaned over, cracked one on the first try, and handed the shell back like a trophy. Deacon tried the other, winced, and gave up. It sat there, hard and brown and untouchable.

"Wait," Ellie said. She was remembering the summer she'd spent at her aunt's farm, the year it barely rained. The pasture had gone crispy by July, and the seed heads on the weeds had dried into little wooden knots. The sparrows that had swarmed the bird feeder in June vanished. But every evening, a few stragglers worked the tough heads by the fence, the ones with thick, heavy bills, and they pried those knots open while everything else went hungry. Her aunt had called them her ugly survivors. At the time Ellie had thought it was just luck, some birds happening to find the good spot. Now she turned the last sunflower seed over in her fingers and thought: it wasn't the spot. It was the beak.

That night she dumped a box of mixed seed on her desk and sorted it with tweezers, role-playing with a binder clip and a pair of needle-nose pliers standing in for different beaks. The pliers cracked the big seeds. The binder clip, her small-beaked finch, could only manage the tiny ones. Then she swept the tiny ones into her drawer. Drought. Small seeds gone. The binder clip starved on paper while the pliers went on eating.

On Friday she stood at the front with the skeleton beside her and her voice only shook twice. She told them about Daphne Major, a small island, and the severe drought of 1977. "When the small seeds ran out," she said, "only the big, hard ones were left. The medium ground finches with larger, deeper beaks could crack them, so those birds survived better. Everyone with the smaller beaks didn't." She held up her binder clip and her pliers. "Same island. Same birds. Different beaks. That's natural selection, and nobody chose it. The drought did the choosing."

Ms. Wijaya wrote one word on the board and underlined it. Jake raised his hand. "Can I be the pliers?"

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: In Shakespeare's English, anon means at once or soon, so a servant calling "Anon!" is saying "Coming right away!"
story:
The bookshop smelled of dust and old paper, and Mia had the copy of Romeo and Juliet open on the counter because Mr. Asante let her study there after school as long as she didn't touch the register. Monday's assignment was to rewrite a scene in modern English, word for word, sense for sense. She'd managed the insults and the sighing, but one servant kept shouting the same bizarre word at a door, over and over, and she couldn't make it mean anything.

"Anon," she read aloud. "Anon, anon." Blaire looked up from the graphic novel section and frowned. "Maybe it's a name? Like the servant's calling someone named Anon to open up."

Mia tried it. "Anon! Open the door!" That worked for the first shout, maybe, but the servant said it three times in four lines, and the third time he said it alone, with no door mentioned at all. You didn't call a name with nobody answering. There had to be a pattern, some rule underneath, and she couldn't see it. She flipped to the glossary at the back of the book. Anon wasn't there.

"Try the shelf behind you," said Matteo, who had been stacking dictionaries for Mr. Asante all afternoon. "The old ones. If it's not in the school copy, it might be somewhere else." Mia carried the tiny thread of hope across the shop, past a shelf labelled LANGUAGE, past a shelf where a rodent had clearly chewed the corner of a leather dictionary, to a battered reference book of Shakespeare's words. Her hands slowed as she turned pages, because if this didn't work, the assignment was due in fourteen hours and she had nothing.

There. Anon: at once, soon. She read the entry twice, then a third time, hardly breathing. The servant wasn't calling anyone. A servant calling "Anon!" was saying "Coming right away!" Somebody offstage wanted him, and he was answering the door, the summons, all of it. Every shout fit. She couldn't exactly quantify her certainty, but four lines that had been nonsense now clicked together like a lock, and she scribbled the paraphrase fast before it could come apart again.

Back at the counter, Blaire leaned over her shoulder. "So what did it mean?" Mia grinned and didn't answer right away. Instead she stood, marched to the shop's front door, and shouted toward the storeroom, "Anon!" From behind the shelves came Mr. Asante's voice, dry and amused: "Yes, yes, coming right away. Though I confess, most of my customers just say hello."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Clothes left crumpled in a dryer or basket after the cycle ends tend to wrinkle as they cool, so taking them out promptly and folding them helps keep them smooth.
story:
The bank's basement smelled like warm paper and lemon soap, which Henry had not expected. His mother, who counted coins in the vault two floors up, had given him permission to use the staff laundry room while she finished her shift, because his older sister had a job interview at this very bank at nine o'clock tomorrow morning and her only good blouse was buried in the hamper. Henry had never done a load by himself. He dumped everything on the folding table and stared at it, wondering where to begin.

Dion arrived first, then Delaney, whose mother also worked upstairs and who folded towels there every Thursday like it was nothing. "Sort darks from lights," Delaney said, picking up a black sock and a pale pink blouse and holding them apart like they were arguing. "Or your whites turn gray." Dion dismissed this immediately. "One load, one cycle, done." But Delaney pointed at a shirt of his that had gone pink last spring, and Dion quietly started making two piles.

Henry asked questions as he worked. Why this dial? Why that slot for the soap? He liked the way the machines had rules you couldn't see, hidden habits that only showed up in the results. The dryer's silver vent hose coiled behind it like an intestine, and he traced it with his eyes until Delaney laughed at him.

Then the trouble started. Delaney had to leave, Dion got called upstairs, and Henry, waiting for the dryer, sat down on a crate of deposit slips and fell asleep. He woke to the cold hum of a finished machine. The blouse was still inside, crumpled against the drum, and when he pulled it out it was crosshatched with deep creases, sharp as folded paper. He ironed it with his hands, then with a water bottle, then with a biology textbook. Nothing worked. Were the wrinkles set because it had sat there, balled up, while it cooled? He looked at the clock. Eight at night. The interview was imminent, and his sister was already asleep at home, trusting him.

He decided to test the idea. He rewashed the blouse alone, and this time he stood in front of the dryer for the whole final ten minutes, watching the drum turn like a scientist watching an experiment he couldn't see inside. The moment the cycle clicked off, he opened the door, shook the blouse out, laid it flat, and folded it carefully along its seams while it was still warm. He hung his face over it, curious, breathing the heat.

In the morning his sister pressed the folded blouse flat on the table, held it up to the light, and raised her eyebrows at him. "It's smooth," she said. "Like, actually smooth." Henry shrugged, but he was already thinking about the second load waiting in his hamper at home. "Next time," he said, "I'm setting a timer."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population.
story:
Elliot had forty minutes before the festival's heritage booth closed, and his graph was wrong. He spread the paper on the folding table beside the stage, where drummers were tuning up and the smell of fried dough drifted from the food tents. The graph showed the origins people in his town had written on the community survey: Scottish, 24 percent; Chinese, 18; Punjabi, 15; Filipino, 12; Irish, 11; Ukrainian, 10; and a long tail of smaller numbers. He added them twice on his calculator and got 128 percent. His teacher, Mr. Tan, wanted the finished poster for the display wall by the time the evening crowd arrived.

"You look like your math exploded," said Cael, leaning over the table. Cayson crowded in beside him, holding a paper plate of samosas.

"My town can't be 128 percent anything," Elliot said. He tapped the calculator. "Somebody must have made a mistake."

They were still arguing about it when a woman at the booth behind them called out, "Origins table! Write up your roots, one per line!" People were scribbling on cards and pinning them to a corkboard. Elliot watched an old man write Scottish and Cree on two lines. A girl his age wrote Chinese, Irish, and Jamaican on three. Cael wrote Trinidadian and Portuguese. Cayson hesitated over his card, then printed Guyanese, Indian, and Dutch, and said, "I never know which one to put first."

Elliot stared at the corkboard. Nobody was picking just one. That was the pattern. It wasn't a math mistake at all; each person could count as more than one origin, so the totals could climb past the population. He tried to think how to check it. His survey asked the same question the Canadian census asked, and he remembered his father grumbling last spring about filling it in. He ran to the information tent, found the census flyer in the recycling bin, and read the fine print until he found it: people had been allowed to report more than one origin since 1981. He looked at the corkboard again. It wasn't a paradox, really; it was just counting people twice because they belonged to more than one place.

"That's it," he told Cael and Cayson, wiping chalk dust off his hands. "The percentages are supposed to add up to more than a hundred." He recalibrated his poster, writing at the top: "Origins reported. People can list more than one, so totals go over 100%." Then he added a column showing how many people had written two or three.

Mr. Tan walked over at five o'clock sharp, read the poster, and smiled. "You solved it yourself?"

"Had to," Elliot said. "Nobody would tell me, and the wall was filling up."

He carried the poster to the display wall and pinned it between a quilt and a map of the world, right under the stage lights. Cayson handed him the last samosa. "For the graph guy," he said, "one hundred and twenty-eight percent of a snack."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, bowing is a common greeting, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows.
story:
Alyssa had wanted the solo in the spring concert ever since October, when she had frozen halfway through her audition and Ms. Levy had gently said, "Next year, maybe." This year the list went up on Monday, and her name was on it, along with Ariyah's and exactly four others. Ms. Levy had to restrict the list to six because the whole period would be taken up by auditions, so every slot mattered.

The new girl, Lucie, was trying out too. She had arrived from Japan in January, and this week her grandparents were visiting the school. Alyssa spotted them outside the office on Wednesday: an old man and woman standing very straight. When Ms. Levy came out to greet them, they bowed, and Lucie's grandfather bowed lower and held it longer than his wife did. When the principal hurried past with a wave, both grandparents bowed again, but shallow and quick. Alyssa chewed her pencil. There was a pattern here, like a code. The important people got the deep, slow bows. She remembered her own grandmother back in the summer, teaching her to look dinner guests in the eye and shake hands firmly, and how Alyssa had decided that must be the one right way everywhere. Now she wasn't so sure.

At lunch, Ariyah slid her tray over next to Lucie's and immediately started talking with her mouth full, the way she always did at home. Lucie kept her lips closed while chewing and held her rice bowl up in one hand, close to her chest. Ariyah caught Alyssa's eye and slowed down, then quietly picked up her own bowl and lifted it, copying her. Lucie's whole face brightened.

When the grandparents came to the music room after school, Lucie carried a small wrapped box to Ms. Levy, holding it out with both hands. Ms. Levy opened it right away, exclaiming over the tea inside, but Lucie's grandmother kept her little parcel sealed, turning it over in her fingers. Lucie leaned toward Alyssa and whispered, "In Japan, bowing is a greeting, and the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows." So the code was real. Alyssa filed that away like a lucky coin.

Alyssa had been rehearsing a stiff little nod for the grandparents, the polite kind she used for strangers. Standing there, she changed her mind. When Lucie's grandfather turned to her, Alyssa bent from the waist, slow and low, and held it while she counted three heartbeats. When she straightened up, he was smiling, and so was Lucie.

At the audition on Friday, Alyssa's voice shook on the first line and then found its footing. Afterward, Lucie caught her in the hallway and bowed, quick and light, the way friends do.

"Deeper than that," Alyssa said, and bowed back so low her hair swung forward.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, 'yes, and' means accepting what your partner has established (yes) and then adding something new to it (and).
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and old basketballs, and Mr. Rahimi had pushed the mats against the wall to make a stage. "Improv," he announced, "is a conversation with no plan. Find a partner."

Anna grabbed Malcolm, mostly because he was standing nearest. Their first scene fell apart in eleven seconds. Anna opened a pretend door and said, "We've landed on Mars." Malcolm said, "Okay." She waited. He said, "Yep, we sure have." The scene lay there like a dropped gym bag until Mr. Rahimi called time.

"What do we do with an offer like Mars?" Mr. Rahimi asked, and when nobody answered, he only smiled and said, "Watch." He didn't explain, which Anna found annoying and, later, grateful for.

Second try, same problem. Anna tried, "Grandma, the horse got into the house again." Malcolm said, "Right." She said, "You have to help me catch him!" Malcolm said, "I agree." The horse stayed invisible and uncaptured. Across the gym, Reet and her partner were building a scene about a bank robbery, talking over each other, laughing, adding spies, adding a getaway submarine. Anna watched them and felt her ears go hot.

She walked it backward in her head. In Reet's scene, every line picked up what the last person said and then made it bigger. In hers, Malcolm said yes to everything, and she presumed the problem was him being lazy, but Reet's partner wasn't more talented, just doing something Malcolm wasn't. The scenes weren't stalling because nobody agreed. They were stalling because Malcolm agreed and then stopped. She tested the idea out loud, quietly, like poking a sore tooth. "It's not the yes. It's what comes after the yes."

"Try again," she told Malcolm. "When I say something, say yes, and then add something. Anything. Say the whole thing, 'yes, and,' then a new piece."

"Feels weird," Malcolm said, but he stood up straighter, which Anna took as a good sign.

"Grandma, the horse got into the house again," she said.

"Yes, and he's eating your retirement fund," Malcolm said. "Every carrot you saved for your pension. The stable out back is empty. He's living in the pantry now, and he looks stable in there, honestly, like he pays rent."

Anna laughed so hard she forgot her next line, and that turned out to be fine, because Malcolm kept going, describing the horse's bathrobe, and she jumped back in with, "Then we charge him rent," and suddenly the scene was a thing with legs, running somewhere on its own.

When Mr. Rahimi called time, he was grinning. "That," he said, pointing, "is what I wanted you to find."

Malcolm offered Anna a pretend high five. She slapped it.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing 'Deaf' with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase 'deaf' for the hearing condition itself.
story:
Cooper stood in the art room with a brush dripping orange paint, staring at the half-finished poster for the sign-language club. Delia had asked him to make it because he had the best handwriting in eighth grade, and because the club's Open Night was Thursday. The poster said WELCOME TO THE DEAF CLUB in molten-looking letters, the way a lava lamp might write if it could hold a brush. Then Marc-Olivier, who ran the club, tapped the poster and frowned. "Lowercase," he signed, and Delia translated. Cooper gaped at him. He had checked his spelling twice. Something invisible was going on, some rule he couldn't see, and he hated not knowing a rule.

After school he found Marc-Olivier in the library and wrote his question on a napkin: why lowercase? What was wrong with capital letters? Marc-Olivier grinned, took the napkin, and wrote back: big D, little d, two different things. Then he slid a book across the table, open to a marked page, and left to meet his bus. Cooper read it twice. In 1972, a linguist named James Woodward had proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase deaf for the hearing condition itself. Cooper sat back. So the poster hadn't been spelling-wrong, it had been meaning-wrong. Big D Deaf was a whole culture, like being Italian or a chess player. Little d was just a category on an audiogram, a way doctors could categorize ears. His poster had accidentally said "welcome to the condition of not hearing" instead of "welcome to the culture."

He tested the idea on Delia in the hallway the next morning. "So if I write Deaf with a big D, I mean the community?" Delia nodded, then laughed so hard she had to lean on a locker. "You should have seen your face yesterday. Like we'd told you the alphabet changed overnight." "It kind of did," Cooper said, which only made her laugh harder. He didn't mind. Being the joke was worth it if he got the rule right.

He remade the poster that evening, painting DEAF in gold capital letters the size of his hand, and underneath, in smaller script, everyone welcome, no hearing required. Around the border he drew hands mid-sign, because Marc-Olivier had once shown him the sign for "connect" and it looked like two hooks linking fingers. He added a speech bubble from one hand that said, simply, "Deaf," big D and all.

Thursday night, Ms. Tehrani, who supervised the club, hung the poster by the door where everyone entering would walk past it. Marc-Olivier stood beside it during Open Night, and when a nervous sixth grader hovered at the entrance, Marc-Olivier pointed at the golden word, then at himself, then at the empty chair next to Cooper. The sixth grader sat down. Cooper, who had learned exactly three signs so far and messed one of them up twice, carefully made the sign for "hello." The sixth grader grinned and signed it back, better than his. "Show-off," Cooper said out loud, and half the club laughed, and Marc-Olivier raised both hands in the sign Cooper was starting to think of as the club's real currency: hands moving, everyone in.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, which slowed the motion enough for him to time it.
story:
Alexander wanted to prove that a ball rolling down the picnic-table ramp got faster as it went, but every time he tried to time it, the ball reached the fence before his thumb could even hit the button on the stopwatch. He had tried three times that afternoon, and the numbers on the screen fluctuated wildly, once 0.8 seconds, once 1.4, once something so short he knew he had missed the start.

"You need the ball to go slower," Flavie said, sitting on the fence rail with the clipboard of graph paper balanced on her knee. She and Kellan had come over because Alexander had promised them a real experiment, not just watching him fail alone.

"Slower balls don't show anything," Alexander said. "I need speed."

"You need time," Kellan said. He was holding the ball, a dented tennis ball that had lost most of its fuzz. "If you can't catch it with the stopwatch, the speed doesn't matter."

Alexander stared at the ramp, which was really just a board propped on two bricks. Something tickled at the back of his mind, a plaque he had read at the science museum in town. There was a long gentle ramp there with a brass ball, and a sign beside it. He closed his eyes and tried to remember the words. "Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps," he said slowly, "which slowed the motion enough for him to time it." He opened his eyes. "That's why the museum ramp is so flat. A gentle slope slows the whole thing down."

"Then make yours gentle," Flavie said.

They rebuilt the ramp. Alexander took away one brick so the board lay at a slant so shallow it looked almost level, and the tennis ball crept down it like a sleepy beetle. He marked the board at every half metre with leftover paint from the garage, and Kellan's job was to call out each mark as the ball crossed it while Alexander worked the stopwatch.

The first run still gave messy numbers, because Kellan called "now" a beat late. The second run fractured into confusion when the ball wobbled off the board entirely. "Again," Flavie said, and Alexander just nodded, because the third time he kept his eyes on the marks instead of the ball, and something clicked. The first half metre took one whole second. The second half metre took less. Each mark after that came faster than the one before, and when Flavie plotted the times on her graph, the dots curved upward in a smooth sweep.

"It's speeding up," Alexander said, looking at the line that bent like a river bending. "The whole run, the whole time."

Mr. Hosseini leaned over the back fence, watering can still in his hand. "What's that you've got?"

"A distance-time graph," Alexander said. "We ran it four more times and the curve stayed consistent." He held up the clipboard. "Every single time, the ball rolls faster the farther it goes."

Mr. Hosseini squinted at the sweeping line and then smiled. "Galileo would have liked that graph."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Blocking is rejecting or ignoring a partner's offer, such as saying 'we're not on a boat', and it usually stops the scene from moving forward.
story:
Willow stood at the edge of the drama room with her hands jammed in her hoodie pocket, hoping the floor would swallow her before Ms. Martínez called her up. It did not. "Willow and Everly, you're next. Two minutes, and remember the rule: accept every offer."

Two minutes felt like two years. Everly bounced onto the mat and immediately planted her feet like an astronaut claiming a planet. "We're on a pirate ship," she announced, "and a storm is coming."

Willow's brain went blank as a wiped whiteboard. Then, out of panic, she heard herself say, "No we're not. We're in the cafeteria."

The room went quiet in a strange, heavy way. Everly's arms dropped to her sides. There was nothing to do, nowhere to go, because Willow had just declared away the only thing they had. They stood there for ten endless seconds until Ms. Martínez said, "Let's reset."

Back in line, Willow chewed her lip and tried to digest what had just happened. It hadn't been embarrassment that killed the scene, or bad acting. It was something simpler. She scanned her memory of the last few pairs: Natasha had opened a scene as an artisan selling magic pottery, and her partner had said, "That's not pottery, it's math class," and the scene had fallen flat, same as Willow's. But when someone had accepted the pottery and haggled over a soup bowl, the scene had stretched like elastic, bending anywhere the actors wanted.

A pattern, Willow thought. A rule you couldn't see but could test. When somebody rejected or ignored what their partner offered, the scene just stopped.

She leaned toward Natasha. "Blocking," Natasha whispered, like she was naming a spell. "Saying 'we're not on a boat' to your partner. That's blocking."

When their turn came again, Everly squared up. "We're on a pirate ship, and a storm is coming."

"Yes," Willow said, grabbing an invisible rope with both hands, "and the captain just fell overboard, so I'm promoting myself. You're the new captain. Congratulations."

Everly's whole face lit up like a struck match. "Yes, and my first order is that the storm is actually a giant sea turtle, and we're riding her to shore." She flung her arm around Willow's shoulders and steered their imaginary deck through waves that got taller and stranger, full of singing jellyfish and an octopus auctioning off the ship's anchor. Willow discovered that if she said "yes, and" to even the silliest offer, the scene grew by itself, like it had been waiting in the dark for someone to open a door.

At the end, the class clapped, and Ms. Martínez wrote one word on the board: BLOCKING, with a line through it.

Walking out, Natasha caught up to them. "So, jellyfish choir," she said. "Rehearsal at lunch?"

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell.
story:
Hudson had counted his money twice in the food court, and both times it came to six dollars and thirty-five cents. His little sister's birthday was on Saturday, and she wanted strawberry shortcake, the real kind, the kind their grandmother used to make. Strawberries at the grocery store in the mall cost five dollars for a small box, which would leave him nothing for cream.

"Buy her a card," said Willyam, who was working his way through a giant pretzel. "Cards say everything cakes say, minus the cake."

"That's not a real sentence," Hudson said, but he was barely listening. He kept thinking about the farmers' market that set up in the mall's north wing every Friday, near the entrance by the old movie theater. Last month he'd walked past a farmer there selling strawberries for four dollars a box, which had seemed outrageous at the time.

He and Dan wandered that way after school, mostly to escape the tedious homework waiting at home, and partly because Hudson wanted to see the stalls again. The mall was warm, and Dan complained about it until Hudson pointed out that at least nobody here controlled the thermostat, unlike in Mr. Vogel's classroom, which was either an icebox or a sauna.

The market smelled like bread and soil. Hudson passed a table of honey, a table of jam, and then he saw them: quarts of strawberries, red all the way to the stem, stacked in flat crates behind a farmer with sunburned arms. A hand-lettered sign read TWO DOLLARS A QUART.

"A month ago these were four dollars for half this much," Hudson said to Dan. "That's half the price. Why would they get cheaper?"

Dan shrugged, but Hudson couldn't let it go. He watched the farmer. The crates went on and on, row after row of them, more strawberries than Hudson had ever seen in one place. Then he noticed the farmer talking to another grower, saying, "I've got more than I can move this week, whole field's coming in."

Hudson turned the thought over. Plenty of something, and the price drops. It was like the opposite of those sneakers everybody wanted last winter, the ones that sold out everywhere and then cost double online. The same hidden rule, running in both directions.

He bought two quarts, then a small carton of cream from the dairy stall with the rest of his money, carefully extracting the exact bills from his pocket so he wouldn't drop them on the floor.

On the way out he passed Willyam, still working on the pretzel. Hudson held up the brimming quarts.

"Cards say everything cakes say," Hudson told him, "minus the cake."

Willyam looked at the strawberries, then at his pretzel, and then made a face like a man realizing his mistake. "Save me a slice?"

"Bring your own cream," Hudson said, and headed for the bus.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: In a 2007 study, people kept awake for a whole night showed about 60 percent stronger reactions to upsetting pictures in the amygdala, a brain area that responds to threats.
story:
Ruby had been looking forward to the sleepover at Grandma's house all week, mostly because Ria was coming too, and Grandma's residence had a wraparound porch, a tire swing, and an attic full of old board games. What Ruby had not planned on was the diorama. Ms. Delgado, her teacher, had assigned a model of a river ecosystem due Monday, and Ruby had left half of it undone. So after Grandma went to bed, Ruby and Ria sat cross-legged on the bedroom floor with a flashlight, gluing pebbles and bending pipe cleaners into cattails until the sky outside turned grey.

"Done," Ria whispered at last, and they fell asleep just as the birds started up.

They got maybe two hours of sleep before Grandma's rooster-shaped clock crowed at seven. At breakfast, Ria nudged the diorama with her elbow and grinned. "Careful, or your barren little river turns into a flood." One tiny pebble slid off the cardboard bank. Ruby snatched the box away, and something hot shot out of her mouth before she could stop it. "Why would you do that? You ruined it! You're always messing with my stuff!"

Ria's face went pale and still. "It was one pebble, Ruby. I was joking." She carried her plate to the sink and went out to the porch alone, shoulders hunched.

Ruby stared at the pebble on the floor. Ria had glued a hundred of those pebbles in place last night, staying up just as late as Ruby had, and now Ruby had yelled at her over one. She found Grandma folding towels in the hallway and asked, quietly, why everything felt so enormous this morning, like her skin was two sizes too small. Grandma didn't lecture. She just handed Ruby a science magazine from the pile by her chair and said, "Page fourteen might interest you."

Ruby read page fourteen twice, then carried it out to the porch. She sat down next to Ria, who was moodily peeling the label off a water bottle. "Listen to this," Ruby said, and read aloud: "'In a 2007 study, people kept awake for a whole night showed about 60 percent stronger reactions to upsetting pictures in the amygdala.'" She lowered the magazine. "That's a brain area that responds to threats. So a picture of one lost pebble felt like a landslide. Not because you did anything wrong. Because my brain is running on no sleep."

Ria considered this. "So the test would be, if you slept, the pebble would go back to being just a pebble?"

"Exactly," Ruby said. "Tonight, actual sleep. No flashlight, no projects. And right now, I'm going to try the breathing thing before I yell at anything else."

She breathed in slowly through her nose for four counts, held it, and let it out for six, the way they'd practiced in gym class, while Ria counted along in a stage whisper. After three rounds, Ruby's shoulders came down from around her ears. She picked up the pebble, walked to the diorama, and pressed it back onto the riverbank with a dab of glue.

"For the record," Ria said, "your river looks better than mine ever did."

That night they were both asleep before ten, and in the morning Ruby woke to the smell of pancakes and found that Ria had already straightened the diorama box so it faced the window, catching the light.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: In Spanish, the masculine plural "hermanos" can mean brothers, or brothers and sisters together, so "Tengo dos hermanos" might describe one brother and one sister.
story:
The quiz was in ten minutes, and Cooper still could not describe his family in Spanish without his notes. Ms. Oyelaran had promised it would be oral: each student standing up, saying five full sentences about their household, no paper allowed. Ten minutes. He paced the hallway outside the language room, whispering, "Tengo un hermano. Tengo un perro."

Wassim sat on the floor against the lockers, frowning at his own hand. "I'm stuck on my sister's line. She's in seventh grade and she practiced with me last night, and she said, 'Tengo dos hermanos.' Which is wrong, right? She has one brother. One. Me."

Cooper stopped pacing. "That's what I thought too. But wait." He crouched down, holding up his fingers like he was working a math problem. "Remember Monday, when Ms. Oyelaran wrote 'tres hermanos' about that family with two boys and a girl? I asked her after class and she just smiled and said, 'Brothers.'" He counted on his fingers again, slower this time. "So maybe hermanos means brothers, or brothers and sisters together. Mixed group, one word. Your sister isn't wrong. Tengo dos hermanos could be one brother and one sister."

Wassim stared at him. "So when I stand up and say I have two hermanos, Ms. Oyelaran won't know if I have a brother or a brother and a sister?"

"Or two brothers!" Cooper was grinning now, the kind of grin that made Wassim laugh even though the quiz was imminent and neither of them had finished practicing. "It's like a mystery you can say in one sentence."

They drilled each other down the hall until the bell. "Mi perro se llama Biscuit," Cooper recited. "Tengo un hermano y una hermana. Vivo con mis padres y mi abuela." The words came faster each round, and his nervousness seemed to dissolve into plain excitement.

Inside the room, the radiators clanked and a thin vapor of steam rose from the coffee cup on Ms. Oyelaran's desk while she called names. Wassim went first. He stood, took a breath, and said, "Tengo dos hermanos. Una hermana y un hermano." Then he looked straight at Cooper and added, "Uno de ellos está en esta clase."

Ms. Oyelaran raised her eyebrows. "Muy bien, Wassim. Y muy valiente." Cooper laughed so hard he nearly fell out of his chair, and she called his name next.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: In Shakespeare's English, a line beginning "Would that" expresses a wish, so "Would that it were so" means "I wish it were so".
story:
Piper spread the photocopy of the Romeo and Juliet scene across the library table and read the same line for the fifth time. "Would that it were so." She said it out loud, then frowned. Was it a question? It started with "would," so maybe it was. The trouble was that the sentence after it didn't answer anything, which made the whole speech feel like a conversation with a hole in it.

She was supposed to paraphrase the scene into modern English for Ms. Sutherland's reading group by Thursday, and so far she had two words down on her paper: "Would???" Across the table, her friend Skyler was hunched over a poster board covered with drawings of moldy bread. Skyler wanted to win the district science fair, and she was trying to prove that her fungus samples had grown faster in the dark cabinet than on the sunny windowsill at home.

"Skyler, you're good at old stuff. What does 'Would that it were so' mean?"

Skyler squinted at Piper's page without lifting her pen from her poster. "No idea. Isn't it asking something, like 'Would you do that?'"

That was Piper's first thought too, so she wrote it down that way: "Would you make it so?" She read the paraphrase back to herself and shook her head. The character in the scene was alone, talking about his friend who had been banished from the city. Nobody was there to ask. A question to an empty room made no sense, and the more Piper read the speech, the more it sounded like longing. "That heaven finds means to kill your joys with love," he said. He wasn't asking. He was grieving.

Piper turned to her notebook and tried an experiment. If "would that" wasn't a question, what if the whole phrase meant the character wanted something? She crossed out her first try and wrote, "I wish it were so." Then she read the line and the paraphrase one after the other, back and forth, three times. The wish fit every time, like the last puzzle piece that sits loose until you rotate it the right way. She flipped to another scene at the back of the packet and found "Would that I were a glove upon that hand." I wish I were a glove on that hand. It worked there too. It was a pattern, not a lucky guess.

She was still testing it when Farah dropped into the chair beside her, slurping a smoothie. "Why do you look like you just discovered a secret door?"

"Would that means I wish," Piper said. "It's not a question at all. It's like Shakespeare's way of saying he's hoping for something impossible."

Farah borrowed the packet and read for a minute, lips moving. Then she grinned. "Okay, that actually makes these speeches easier. Can I try paraphrasing the next one? I've been pretending Shakespeare was boring so nobody would ask me to read out loud, but if it's just translating, I can do translating."

Piper slid the packet across the table, and while Farah wrote, Ms. Sutherland stopped beside them on her rounds with a cart of returns. She read Piper's crossed-out first attempt and the corrected second one, and nodded at the crossed-out version. "Keeping your mistakes in your notes is a good habit. It shows you how your thinking grew."

Skyler looked up from her poster then and studied Piper's page for a long moment. "You know what, my fungus project is about how things grow better in the dark. Maybe my display should show the failed windowsill batch too, instead of hiding it." She pulled out a fresh sheet and began sketching a second row of samples. Piper picked up her pen, wrote "I wish it were so" neatly at the top of her paraphrase, and started on the next line before she could lose the rhythm.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Ritardando, often written rit., means gradually slowing down, and accelerando means gradually speeding up.
story:
Gabriel had been playing trumpet in the school band for exactly three weeks, which was long enough to hit most of the notes and short enough to be dangerous. Mr. Sandhu had handed out a new piece called "Storm Chase" and told them all to mark their music carefully, especially measure forty-two. Gabriel squinted at the page. Above measure forty-two sat three tiny letters: r-i-t.

At rehearsal the next morning, the whole band reached measure forty-two and the sound split in half. The trumpets and the drums barreled ahead at full speed, while the flutes and the clarinets slowed way down, stretching the notes like taffy. The result was so terrible that Reid, who played baritone, laughed so hard he honked into his mouthpiece by accident, which sounded like a dying goose and made it worse.

"Someone is going to get humiliated at the concert," Dane whispered to Gabriel as Mr. Sandhu lowered his baton. "Possibly all of us. Simultaneously."

Gabriel stared at his music. He noticed that the flute players had all written something in pencil next to the letters, and the trumpet players mostly hadn't. That was a pattern. Flutes read it one way, trumpets read it another, and the answer had to be in those three letters. He borrowed a flute player's music at lunch and compared it to his own, piece by piece, like a census of every pencil mark in the band.

That night, a folded note appeared in his trumpet case. In Dane's handwriting it said: "Dear Gabriel. Reid bet me two cookies that you can't fix the rit. problem by Friday. I bet three cookies that you can, because you stare at things until they confess. Do not let me down, and do not eat my cookies. Signed, Dane. P.S. Reid says hi."

Friday morning, Gabriel stood up before rehearsal started. "I did a count," he announced. "Nine of us marked our music and six of us didn't. The rit. means gradually slowing down, so the people who ignored it kept going at the same speed. We're not bad, we're just reading two different maps."

"Then what about the other word?" Reid called out, pointing at measure fifty-eight, where a long squiggle of a word sat above the staff. "Accelerando. What does that one do?"

Gabriel looked at the shape of the word, long and leaning forward, and thought about how rit. pulled the sound backward. "It's the opposite," he said. "Gradually speeding up." He wasn't guessing, exactly, but he wasn't certain either, and his stomach felt volatile, like it might flip either direction.

Mr. Sandhu tapped his stand twice. "Then let's test it. Everyone marks measure fifty-eight. Flutes, don't be smug, half of you are wrong there too."

They played the whole passage. At measure forty-two the band slowed together, smooth as a wave, and at fifty-eight they gathered speed like a snowball rolling downhill. When the last note cut off, the room was silent for one whole second, and then Dane stood up on his chair and held his trumpet over his head like a trophy.

"Three cookies!" he shouted. "Pay up, Reid!"

Reid reached into his backpack and pulled out a crumpled paper bag. "Fine. But you're sharing."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death', so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor.
story:
The scavenger hunt list said the raffle drum would spin at four o'clock sharp, and Camille had forty minutes to find the last two items: a lucky envelope and an elevator that lied. "An elevator that lies?" Chance said, squinting at the paper while the smell of frying scallion pancakes drifted past. "That can't be right." Ms. Quinn, running the welcome table, pressed a red envelope into Camille's hands with both of her own and gave a small bow, which Camille returned, remembering to keep her elbows off the table later when they sampled dumplings at Mehdi's family booth, where his grandmother gestured for them to take the middle seats, never the ones facing the door.

The elevator part made sense once Camille thought about it. The hunt was happening in the Sun Tower, the apartment building attached to the festival grounds, and her grandmother had once mentioned that buildings sometimes told small fibs with their numbers. In the lobby, Camille rode up with Mehdi, watching the buttons light up in order: three, five, six. She counted the floors as they passed, and the numbers outside the elevator doors jumped the same way, three to five, like a skipped heartbeat.

She had an idea, and it was simple enough to test. "Get off with me at five," she said. "We'll walk down one flight and see what's really there." Mehdi shrugged and followed. The stairwell door opened onto a corridor with a painted five on the wall, and the floor below it, where a four should have been, was labelled five as well. The building simply had no four, as if it had decomposed into a gap and been swept away.

"That's the one," Camille said, pulling out the clue sheet. "Find a floor that doesn't exist." Mehdi laughed. "My aunt lives in a building like this in Shanghai," he said. "In Chinese, the word for four sounds very similar to the word for death, so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor." He said it lightly, the way he'd say the sky was blue, and Camille wrote it down because the hunt asked for the reason too.

They ran back down, and on the way Camille stopped at Mehdi's booth to wrap a few dumplings in napkins for Chance, who hadn't eaten anything and was looking pale in the heat. The elastic band on her wrist snapped twice as she stretched it over the container, but it held.

They reached the raffle table at 3:58, and Ms. Quinn stamped their sheet just as the drum began to turn. "Floor that doesn't exist," she read, smiling. "Took you long enough. Nobody ever looks up in an elevator."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Crying when a parent leaves is called separation anxiety; it is a normal stage of development that commonly begins in the second half of a baby's first year.
story:
Parker had expected babysitting to be easy money. He had not expected the baby to scream the second the parents walked out the door.

"Can you make her stop?" asked Saif, who had come along because Parker's mom said not to go alone. He was standing on a chair, as though the screaming were something that could climb.

The baby's name was Ruby, eight months old, and she was turning a color Parker had previously seen only on tomatoes. He bounced her. He sang a song about a bus. He showed her his keys, which interested her for exactly one second before the wailing resumed. In the corner of the living room sat a diaper bag, and beside it a paperback with a cracked spine, the kind of book parents read in eight-second bursts. Parker picked it up one-handed and flipped pages while Ruby howled into his shoulder.

There it was, on page 114. Crying when a parent leaves is called separation anxiety, and it is a normal stage of development that commonly begins in the second half of a baby's first year. It said the crying usually fades once a distraction begins. Parker had assumed the screaming meant he had done something wrong, like a burglar alarm he had tripped somehow. Instead it was just a stage. A loud, normal stage.

"So she's not broken," he told Saif. "It's a stage."

"Can we return her to the stage she was before?"

Parker ignored this. He needed a distraction, and it needed to be good. The book suggested peekaboo, but Ruby could not see his hands from inside her own tantrum. He looked around the room instead. The curtains were camouflage-green, the exact color of his uncle's hunting jacket, and behind them the window looked out on an arid patch of yard where a sprinkler dragged its slow arc across the grass. Water. Babies liked water.

He carried Ruby to the window and pulled the curtain back. Nothing. Then the sprinkler swept past the glass, spraying a fan of drops that caught the afternoon light, and Ruby stopped mid-scream, mouth still open, as if she'd forgotten what the mouth was for.

"Ba," said Ruby.

"Ba," agreed Parker. They stood there through four full sweeps of the sprinkler. By the third one she was laughing, a sound like a small rubber duck being defended.

When the parents came home two hours later, Ruby was asleep in her crib and Parker was on the couch with the book, feeling professional. The mother counted out his pay and glanced at the paperback.

"Did she cry when we left?"

"For a while," Parker said. "Then we watched the sprinkler."

"Separation anxiety," she said. "The sitter before you called it 'the apocalypse.'"

Parker held out his hand for the money. "Book's on page one-fourteen," he said.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: On drawing pencils, H is usually read as 'hardness' and B as 'blackness', so a 6B pencil makes darker, softer marks than a 4H.
story:
Isaac spread his pencils across the kitchen table and checked the clock again. The art contest entries had to be at the community center by four o'clock, and it was already half past two. His drawing, a portrait of his dog Pepper curled on the porch, looked wrong. The shadows were so faint that Pepper seemed to be floating, like a ghost dog.

He frowned at the page. Last night the shading had looked darker. He hadn't changed anything, except that this morning he had knocked the pencil box over and shoved everything back in a hurry.

His friend Cruz arrived, holding a folded note from Billie, who was home with a sprained ankle and couldn't come. Isaac opened it. "You said your dog looks washed out," Billie had written. "Check which pencil you actually grabbed. Not all pencils are the same. My mom got me a whole set and the letters mean opposite things. Billie."

Isaac held his pencil up to the window light. Near the end, in tiny letters, it said 4H. He found another one, a 6B, and made a test stripe with each on the corner of a scrap paper. The 6B went down dark and velvety. The 4H left a mark so pale he could barely see it.

"So that's it," he said. "H must be for hardness. And B is for blackness." He started sorting the whole box, deciding he could categorize them into two groups, the H pile for light lines and the B pile for shadows.

While he worked, Cruz bent the copper wire they were using for the frame of Pepper's collar tag. "This stuff is resilient," Cruz said, snapping it back straight. "You can bend it a hundred times and it doesn't crack. Billie says it's actually an alloy, two metals mixed together."

"Then it can survive the judges," Isaac said. He layered the 6B into the porch shadow under Pepper's chin, then along her back where the evening light faded. The dog sank onto the boards, solid and heavy, exactly the way she looked at dinnertime when she was hoping for scraps.

At ten to four they ran the six blocks to the community center, the drawing in a plastic sleeve, the wire tag jingling against it in Isaac's backpack. The volunteer at the desk pointed to the entry box. Isaac slid his drawing in just as the clock struck four, and Cruz clapped him on the shoulder.

"Ghost dog no more," Cruz said.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: Dopamine release teaches the brain that a behavior is worth repeating, which is how nicotine use becomes a learned habit.
story:
Ellie stood at the bathroom sink outside the gym, index cards fanned in one wet hand, and tried to say it out loud one more time before Mr. Halvorsen called her name. "Dopamine release teaches the brain that a behavior is worth repeating," she whispered to the mirror, "and that's how nicotine use becomes a learned habit." The words kept sliding around like soap. She knew them. She just couldn't make anyone feel them.

The bathroom door banged open and Sirine came in, still holding her phone, thumb already moving. "They moved the science talks to after lunch," Sirine said. "Caiden went first and it was a disaster. He just read his cards." She glanced at the screen, frowned, put the phone face down on the sink ledge, and picked it up again ten seconds later.

"That," Ellie said, pointing. "Do that again."

"Do what?"

"Put it down. Watch how fast you pick it back up."

Sirine rolled her eyes but played along, setting the phone down flat. They both stared at it. Her hand twitched toward it twice before she finally snatched it up, laughing. "Okay, that's invasive, your experiment. And I lost."

Ellie felt something click into place, the way a jar lid does when you finally get the right angle. "Don't you see? Your brain got a little hit of good feeling every time you checked for likes. Dopamine. It teaches your brain that checking is worth repeating, so it turns into a habit you don't even decide on." She flipped a card over. "Nicotine does the same thing. The dopamine release teaches the brain that nicotine is worth repeating, and that's how it becomes a learned habit. It's not weakness. It's learning."

Sirine leaned against the stall door, quiet for a moment. "Last week I told my brother he was pathetic for vaping. He tried to quit twice and I said he just didn't really want to." She picked at the edge of Ellie's card. "Maybe wanting isn't the whole thing. Maybe I was judging him for something his brain got taught." She didn't say sorry out loud, but she looked like she was thinking about texting him.

"I was going to stand up there and read cards like Caiden," Ellie said. She dropped the whole stack into the trash can, one by one, like dealing out a hand. "My mom would have to authorize a search party to find my grade after that."

"You're just going to talk?"

"I'm going to talk about her." Ellie nodded at the phone in Sirine's hand. "You're going to lend me your lock screen, and I'm going to make everyone watch your thumb."

Sirine clutched the phone to her chest. "Never. We'd have to sign a treaty."

"Two weeks of me carrying your backpack," Ellie said. "Final offer."

The bell rang down the hall. Sirine held out the phone. "Deal," she said. "Go make Caiden cry."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: A crescendo means gradually getting louder, and a diminuendo or decrescendo means gradually getting softer.
story:
The flyer on the community centre bulletin board said FREE COMMUNITY BAND, ALL LEVELS, and Quinn had taken that as a personal dare. She'd been playing piano since second grade, but only alone, in her living room, where nobody could hear her mistakes. Now she sat in the third row of the band room with a borrowed keyboard and a folder of music, wedged between Ayesha on flute and Ayana on trumpet, waiting for something to happen.

Something happened. It was the piece, all right, a real one with parts for everyone, and for the first two pages Quinn kept up fine. Then the sheet music did something sneaky. Under the notes it said crescendo, with one of those long skinny angle shapes opening toward the right, and Quinn, who had never seen one before, made a reasonable guess: this must be the part where you get loud. She got loud. So did everyone else, all at once, like a door slamming.

"Whoa," said Ayana, lowering her trumpet. "We sound like a fire alarm."

Ms. Cardinal, who ran the band, held up her hands. "Let's take that bar again. Gentler this time." She did not say what a crescendo was. She mostly said things like "listen to each other" and "try it again," which was either very wise or a way of drinking her coffee while the band taught itself.

Quinn stared at the angle shape. It started skinny and got wide, like a triangle lying on its side, opening up as the music went along. She had guessed "loud," but maybe the shape was the instruction itself, not just a decoration. Gradually getting louder, widening bit by bit, instead of everyone jumping to loud at once like the whole band had been startled by the same bee. She flipped the page and found the shape going the other way, closing down toward skinny, marked diminuendo. If one shape meant gradually louder, the mirror of it probably meant gradually softer. Opposite directions, opposite results. It was almost annoying how sensible that was.

She leaned over to Ayesha. "So crescendo means gradually louder, right? Not just loud."

"Gradually louder," Ayesha confirmed. "And diminuendo is the opposite, gradually softer. Decrescendo too, same thing, they just gave it two names because apparently one wasn't enough."

"Like how we needed two words for trumpet mute and trumpet very muted," Ayana said. "Band is complicated."

They tried the bar again. This time Quinn started quiet and let each measure climb a little louder, and because she was watching Ayesha out of the corner of her eye and Ayesha was doing the same thing, the sound built instead of slammed. When they hit the diminuendo, the whole band eased down together like a tide going out. Ms. Cardinal put down her coffee. That alone felt like a standing ovation.

That night, Quinn texted her grandmother, who had played clarinet in school approximately one hundred years ago.

"Grandma," she wrote, "I was right that crescendo means loud and wrong that it means loud immediately. It means gradually louder, and diminuendo means gradually softer. Also a girl named Ayesha can play flute quietly enough to emphasize a mouse sneeze, which is a legitimate skill."

Her grandmother wrote back within a minute, which meant she had been sitting by her phone. "In my day we called it getting carried away. Proud of you. Did you get your flu vaccine this year? Musicians need lungs."

Quinn laughed, then looked at the sheet music spread across her bed, all triangles and Italian words, and set her alarm ten minutes early to practice the quiet parts. The loud parts, she figured, could take care of themselves.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: The noon Sun climbs higher in the sky in summer than in winter, so shadows at noon are shorter in summer.
story:
Thomas had a fence post, a stick of chalk, and a plan that he hoped would make him sound credible when Ms. Weber asked the seasons question on Monday. The question was, "Explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons," and Thomas suspected that "the Earth tilts, so, seasons" would not earn full marks. He needed proof he could point to.

So he stood in his backyard at noon on a bright June day, holding his mother's kitchen timer because he did not trust himself to notice when exactly noon arrived. When the timer beeped, he chalked the tip of the fence post's shadow onto the patio, measured it with a tape measure, and wrote "June noon: 41 centimeters" in his notebook. His friend Chael watched from a lawn chair, eating chips with the focus of a much older man.

"Forty-one," Thomas said. "Now we wait."

"Until December," Chael said. "That's your whole plan? We sit here and conserve our energy for six months?"

"My adversary is not you," Thomas said. "My adversary is the Sun."

Chael pointed out that the Sun was probably not taking sides. Thomas ignored him, because in December they came back. Zak joined them for the second measurement, mostly for the hot chocolate, and the three of them stood around the fence post in their coats while the timer counted down. At the beep, Thomas chalked the shadow's tip, measured, and wrote the number down twice because he did not believe it the first time.

"One hundred and ninety-two centimeters," Zak read over his shoulder. "That's huge. It goes past the birdbath."

"In June it barely got past the patio," Thomas said. He drew two lines in his notebook, one short, one long, and stared at them. "Same post. Same fence. Same noon." He looked up at the low winter sun, squinting, then flipped back to his June page. "The Sun climbs higher in the sky in summer. That's why the shadow's short. And in winter it stays low, so the shadow stretches out." He tapped the notebook. "That's my proof. A fence post doesn't lie."

"A fence post can't lie," Chael agreed. "It's a fence post. It doesn't do anything."

Zak crouched next to the long chalk mark by the birdbath. "So on Monday, you're going to tell Ms. Weber that the seasons are real because of a fence post?"

"I'm going to tell her the Sun sits higher at noon in summer, and my shadow agrees with me," Thomas said. He closed the notebook, tucked it under his arm, and picked up the tape measure. "Also, we're marking the patio again in March. Someone has to check the in-between."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet; 'most students at our school walk to school' could be tested with a survey.
story:
At dinner on Tuesday, Dad announced that most students at Joseph's school walked to school. He said it the way he said everything, loud and certain, stabbing his fork toward the window for emphasis. Joseph's little sister was pushing peas around her plate, and Mom was already shaking her head, but nobody argued. Joseph set down his glass. "How do you know?" Dad shrugged. "Look at the parking lot. The car line's tiny. It has to be most." Joseph turned his fork over, thinking. "But that's just what you think. It could be checked." His sister rolled her eyes, but Dad leaned back. "Fine. Check it."

The next morning Joseph stood at the front gate with a clipboard and two pencils, because Margot had insisted on a backup. Kate arrived first and grabbed the clipboard. "Are we counting walkers or bus riders?" "Both," Joseph said. "And bikers and car riders. Every student." Margot frowned. "That's the whole school. Nobody's ever done that." "It's checkable," Joseph said, "even if nobody's checked it yet." He had worked that out on the walk over: a thing didn't have to be proven to be provable. They only needed a tally sheet and one morning, or maybe three mornings, in case Wednesday was weird.

Wednesday was weird. A hawk, big and predatory, stooped out of the sky at the soccer field, scattering pigeons, and half the walkers stopped to gawk, which messed up the count. Kate laughed so hard she dropped the clipboard in a puddle. Joseph shared his backup pencil with Margot, whose hands were cold, and lent Kate his jacket sleeve to dry the page. By Thursday they had three clean tally columns and a real answer: 61 percent of students walked. Dad was right. Joseph felt his certainty diminish a little anyway, because it had never been certainty, only a lucky guess.

At Friday dinner, Joseph slid the tally sheet across the table. Dad read it twice. "Sixty-one percent. Huh." He looked almost disappointed. "You know I never checked that," he said quietly. "I just remembered walking when I was your age and figured." Mom smiled at Joseph. "So you proved him right." "I proved it," Joseph said. "He guessed it. Those aren't the same thing." Dad laughed and raised his glass of water to him.

But then Kate texted him a photo of Thursday's sheet, zoomed in on the biker column, and Joseph went still. He had biked on Thursday, for the first time all year, because counting walkers had made him want to try it. Without him, the walking and biking side dropped to 49.5 percent. He had pushed it over "most" himself. He was both the surveyor and, sort of, the result.

At dinner he told Dad the whole thing, and Dad set down his fork and grinned. "So the claim was true because of the kid checking the claim." Joseph's little sister, still pushing peas, said, "That's so weird," and Joseph propped the tally sheet against the salt shaker where everyone could see it. "Next week I'm doing the bus."

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In much of Latin America, a cuadra is a city block, so directions like dos cuadras mean two blocks.
story:
Hayden knocked on Sage's door holding his phone like a ticket to somewhere far away. Sage's grandmother, who everyone called Abuela, was visiting from Mexico for two weeks, and Sage had promised that today they would finally practice real Spanish, not the kind from worksheets.

"My motivation is simple," Sage said, pulling him inside. "If I can talk to Abuela without my mom translating, she'll make us churros every single day of her visit."

The kitchen smelled like cinnamon and hot oil. Abuela was already stirring something on the stove. Hayden's heart hammered. He had one job, and he had practiced the sentence twenty times on the bus: "Dónde está la biblioteca?" Where is the library? It was a game they had invented, because Abuela had never been to their town before and Sage thought asking her for directions would be hilarious, since obviously she did not know either.

Abuela laughed when he asked, then played along anyway. "Dos cuadras," she said, and traced a little square in the air with her spoon. "Una cuadra, dos cuadras. Luego, a la derecha." Hayden nodded fast, thanked her, and jogged outside with Sage to test the answer on the actual streets.

"Two streets, then right," Hayden said, counting intersections. But when they hit the second street and turned, the library was nowhere in sight. They found a laundromat, an eccentric old house painted purple with a wind chime made of spoons, and a dog that barked at them like they owed it money. No library.

"Maybe you heard it wrong," Sage said.

"No, it was dos." Hayden stopped on the sidewalk, frowning. She had traced a square in the air. A square. Like a block. He pictured Abuela's spoon drawing its little outline, and something clicked. "Wait. She didn't mean streets. Una cuadra, two cuadras, blocks. In much of Latin America a cuadra is a city block, so dos cuadras means two blocks." He pointed down the street. "We counted streets, not blocks."

They walked one more block, turned right, and there it was, brick and wide and glowing in the afternoon sun like it had been waiting for them. Sage whooped so loudly that a woman watering her roses looked up.

Back in the kitchen, Hayden asked Abuela, in careful Spanish, whether it was really two blocks. She clapped her hands and said yes, that a cuadra was a block, exactly that. Sage slid into the seat beside her and started a sentence in wobbly Spanish, and Abuela reached for the flour.

"Churros?" she asked, raising one eyebrow.

"Churros," Sage said.

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: The point guard is usually the team's main ball handler and is called the "1" in basketball's numbered positions.
story:
The buzzer hadn't even started the game yet, and Eli was already nervous. Coach had handed him the ball at practice and said, "You're running point today. Play the one." Play the one? Eli had grabbed the ball, nodded like he understood, and spent the whole walk to the court at the park trying to figure out what that could possibly mean.

Last summer flashed back to him as he laced his shoes under the crooked rim at the park court. He'd been the worst kid at Ms. Wanjiru's summer clinic, so bad that she'd made him stand at the free throw line and just mimic her footwork for an entire week, over and over, until his pivot foot stopped sliding all over the place. "You learn with your feet before your hands," she'd said. Maybe learning this new thing would be the same: slow, then sudden.

Miller and Andy jogged onto the blacktop, and Andy was already bouncing a ball off his own forehead. "You're point guard now," Miller said. "So call a play, genius. First game to eleven."

"I'm working on it," Eli said. In his head, he turned the coach's words over. Play the one. The point guard brought the ball up, every time. He was the main ball handler, everyone knew that, and if the coach called it a number, then maybe every spot on the floor had a number, like seats in a theater. The one had to be the spot with the ball.

Andy checked the ball to him and the game began. Eli dribbled left, and Miller stepped out from behind Andy and planted himself like a fence. That was a screen. Eli had seen it a hundred times on TV without knowing it had a name, and now it hit him: the screen was the whole play. He could use Miller's body to shake Andy loose, then Miller could pivot and roll toward the basket, and Eli would dish it to him at the last second. A pick and roll. His cousin had yelled it at a Knicks game once, and Eli had copied it into his memory without knowing what it meant.

He tried it. He drove hard off Miller's hip, dragging Andy with him, then whipped a bounce pass behind him to where Miller should have been rolling. The ball skidded out of bounds. Andy laughed so hard he had to hold his knees. "That was an offense this impoverished," Miller wheezed. "We couldn't even feed ourselves."

"Again," Eli said, gripping the ball. The idea wasn't wrong, he was almost sure of that. The pass had failed because Miller rolled one way while Eli threw the other, and that was a problem you could fix with a signal. "Next time I drive, you roll to the rim. Watch my eyes, not the ball."

They ran it again. Miller set the screen, Eli dragged Andy past it, and this time Miller spun and cut hard to the hoop, exactly on cue. Eli's pass arrived a half second before Andy could recover, soft and low, right into Miller's hands. Layup. Miller screamed like they'd won a championship instead of scoring one basket out of eleven.

"One more," Eli called out, already backing up with the ball, already seeing the whole floor in front of him like a map with numbered streets. "Miller, screen left."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: A person's reaction time on a stopwatch is often about a fifth of a second, so timing a longer run makes that error matter less.
story:
Juliette set the soccer ball at the top of the driveway, where the cement sloped gently toward the garage door. "You time it," she told Jeremiah, holding out her mother's stopwatch. "I'll mark where it stops, and we'll do ten rolls for the graph." She wanted the science extra credit, but she also wanted something that looked like a real hill on graph paper, not the flat line her last attempt had produced.

The first roll went fine. The second one did not. Jeremiah called out "2.4 seconds" while Sabrina, timing the same roll on her phone from the porch, said "2.2 seconds." They argued about it until Juliette held up both hands. "Wait. Same ball, same slope, same moment. One of these numbers is wrong, or both are." She made them time three more rolls together, and every time the stopwatch and the phone disagreed by about a fifth of a second, sometimes one way, sometimes the other.

She sat on the front step with her notebook and stared at the two columns of numbers. It was like the disagreement itself was a clue. "It's us," she said slowly. "Your thumb doesn't press the button the instant you see the ball move. Neither does Sabrina's. Our reaction time is about a fifth of a second, and it's in every single measurement." Jeremiah frowned at the stopwatch as if it had betrayed him personally. "So all our numbers are wrong?" "Not exactly," Juliette said. "But the mistake is the same size no matter what we time. So if we timed something longer, the mistake would matter less."

"We could make the run longer," Sabrina said, already looking down the street, where the sidewalk ran flat and straight for half a block to the stop sign. Juliette grinned. A longer run was harder to roll on, but the numbers would be cleaner, and a clean graph was probable to come out of it, which was more than she could say for the driveway mess.
