"New alliance," she declared. "Same jobs, longer course. And this time I want to replicate each roll at least twice, so we can see if our timings agree."

Mr. Oyelaran, watering his roses next door, watched them chalk a start line at the top of the sidewalk. "Science project?" he asked. "Measuring how fast a ball rolls," Juliette said, "and then drawing it. Distance on one axis, time on the other." He nodded and went back to his roses, but a minute later he called, "My garage has a ramp, if you ever want a steeper one." Juliette said they might take him up on that.

The long rolls worked. When Sabrina's phone said 6.1 seconds and Jeremiah's stopwatch said 6.3, the gap was there but it was small, and the points on Juliette's graph fell into a tidy climbing line. She taped the graph into her notebook and held it up for the others to see. "That," she said, "is our hill." Jeremiah leaned in and traced the line with one finger, from the bottom corner to the top edge of the page.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In the United States, a permanent change of address filed with the Postal Service forwards First-Class Mail to the new address for 12 months.
story:
Sebastian sat on the floor of his half-empty bedroom, surrounded by boxes, holding a stack of letters he had found under his desk. In three days his family would be driving to Rockford, and everything he owned would either come with him or get left behind. He had already said goodbye to Malik and Clemence at school, and the goodbye had felt too short, like a song cut off in the middle.

"What are you doing up there?" his mother called from the hall.

"Packing," Sebastian called back, which was only half true. He was mostly thinking about the mail. His father had filled out the change of address form at the post office that morning, and the clerk had said something Sebastian couldn't stop turning over: a permanent change of address filed with the Postal Service forwards First-Class Mail to the new address for twelve months. Not forever. Twelve months. Which meant the postal system would carry his old life to his new house, but only for a while.

He tested the idea before he trusted it. That evening he wrote a letter to himself, addressed it to the old house on Delancey Street, and dropped it in the corner mailbox with his father. If the rule was real, the letter would leave his old address behind, catch up with him, and land in Rockford. If it was not real, the letter would sit in some dead pile in his old town, and he would know the rule had failed. Then Malik called, and Sebastian asked him to send something too, anything, to the old address. "To the old address?" Malik said. "That's the whole point," Sebastian said. "I want to see what happens."

The first week in Rockford was boxes, new streets, and a grocery store where the cashier recommended what she called a nutritious multigrain bread, which turned out to be better than it sounded. Sebastian kept checking the mailbox even though he told himself not to. Six days, nothing. Eight days, nothing, and he started to think his test had failed, that somewhere in Illinois a letter addressed to a boy who no longer lived there was drifting toward oblivion.

On the ninth day his father handed him an envelope with a yellow sticker on it. The sticker showed his old Delancey Street address crossed out above the new Rockford one, and inside, in Sebastian's own handwriting, was the letter he had mailed to himself before they left. He read his own words, standing at the kitchen counter, feeling like he had caught the postal system in the middle of a secret operation.

Two days later a second envelope arrived, thick and lumpy, forwarded from the old address the same way. Inside was a note from Malik and one from Clemence, plus a flattened penny she had put on the train tracks near school. "In social studies we had to elaborate on a topic for two whole minutes," Malik had written, "so I talked about how moving away doesn't end a friendship, it just changes the address on it. Ms. Thompson said it was the best one."

Sebastian carried the letters up to his new room, set the flattened penny on the windowsill where it would catch the morning light, and started writing his reply.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: In the Koppen climate system, a tropical rainforest climate has every month averaging at least 18 degrees Celsius and at least 60 millimeters of rain.
story:
The tent smelled of pine and damp canvas, and rain ticked against the fabric like a slow clock. Kayla knelt on her sleeping bag with her science folder spread open between the lantern and a bag of trail mix. Mr. Kim had assigned the project before the trip, comparing the climate of a desert and a rainforest, and he had made one thing clear: they had to decide for themselves whether their chosen cities really counted. A thick fog settling over the campsite would have hindered anyone hoping to measure the night sky, but Kayla only needed her graphs.

Estelle unzipped the tent flap, letting in a gust of cool, wet air. "Chad's dad says the rain won't stop till morning," she reported, dropping down beside Kayla. "What are you doing with all that paper?"

"Trying to figure out if Singapore is actually a rainforest climate or if I just picked it because it sounded good." Kayla smoothed the rainfall graph flat. The bars rose in a solid wall, month after month, with no dry gap anywhere. Beside it, the temperature line sat high and almost flat across the whole year.

Chad crawled in after Estelle, shaking water off his jacket. "If it rains that much all year, obviously it's a rainforest," he said, reaching for the trail mix.

"Obviously isn't evidence," Kayla said. She flipped through her notes and found the page she'd copied from the climate chapter, the one Mr. Kim had marked with a sticky note that just said check. At the bottom, in her own handwriting, was the rule: every month had to average at least 18 degrees Celsius, and every month had to have at least 60 millimeters of rain. She read it twice, then held the page up to the lantern.

"So I check each month," she said slowly. "One at a time." She put her finger on January. "Eighty millimeters, twenty-six degrees. Good." February. March. April. Her finger moved down the wall of bars like a climber finding holds. Estelle leaned in and started calling out the numbers for May and June while Chad, without being asked, checked the temperature line for July and August. Somewhere outside, water dripped steadily from a branch onto the tent roof.

Near the end of the stack, Kayla stopped. "February only has sixty-two millimeters." She checked the number again, her pulse quick even though she already knew the answer. "Still over sixty. All twelve months pass." She wrote tropical rainforest climate beside the city name and underlined it, then pulled the desert graph toward her, where Cairo's bars barely rose off the bottom of the page.

"Desert next," she said, tapping the thin little rectangles. "This should take about ten seconds."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In France, friends often greet each other with cheek kisses called 'la bise', and the number of kisses varies from region to region.
story:
Jonathan stood in the doorway of Ms. Andersen's classroom with a bowl of his mother's potato salad clutched against his chest, watching the families file in for the international potluck. His family had lived here only three weeks, since his father's job moved them from Lyon, and tonight was supposed to be the night he finally made friends like Abraham and Riaan, who sat in the back row laughing at something on Riaan's phone.

He remembered his last day in Lyon, when his cousin Élodie had shown up at the farewell party and kissed his cheeks twice, then his uncle Alain had arrived and done it three times, and Jonathan had whispered to Élodie that Uncle Alain must be extra sad about the move. She had laughed so hard she had to sit down. That was the trouble with moving: every place had its own invisible rules, and he could not see them until he broke one.

"Jonathan!" Ms. Andersen waved him toward the long table near the windows. "Put your dish anywhere. Abraham brought his grandmother's dumplings, and Riaan brought samosas." Jonathan set down the bowl and hesitated, because back home you never handed food straight to the host. You set it down and let her admire it first, and his mother had spent ten minutes perfecting the parsley garnish so it would flourish properly, green and bright against the yellow. Here, Abraham's dish had landed on the table like a basketball.

At dinner the differences piled up. Riaan's family ate with their right hands only, bread torn small. Abraham's grandmother refused to let anyone start until the eldest guest had taken the first bite. Jonathan, working these out quietly, kept his hands in his lap between courses, and when Abraham slurped his soup without a single glance from anyone, Jonathan filed that away too. His mother would have gasped.

Then Riaan's older brother walked in late, and Riaan jumped up to greet him with a quick, easy back-slapping hug. Something clicked in Jonathan's mind. Back home, friends greeted each other with cheek kisses, la bise, his mother called it, and the number of kisses changed depending on the region, which was exactly why Élodie had laughed. The rule was invisible, and the only way to find it was to watch and guess and get it wrong.

So when Abraham's cousin arrived, a boy from another town, and stood awkwardly holding his container of cookies, Jonathan did not stick out his hand or go in for a hug. He waited, hands loose at his sides, and let the cousin choose first. The cousin nodded. Jonathan nodded back. "Smart move," Riaan said, leaning over. "Last year some kid high-fived him and he just stared at it like it was a dead fish."

Maybe the greeting rules here were permanent, or maybe they shifted from house to house the way the kisses did back home, from two to three with no warning at all. Jonathan could not be sure, and he decided that was fine. He tore a piece of bread, kept his elbows off the table, and slid the last samosa onto Abraham's plate. "Trade you," he said, "for one of those dumplings."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis.
story:
Ariana spread her poster board across the folding table at the edge of the gymnasium, smoothing the curling corners with her palm. Behind her, eighth graders were hanging banners from the bleachers, and the smell of floor wax mixed with the hot glue someone was using two tables down. Her project measured how high a basketball bounced after being dropped from different heights, and her graph was supposed to be the crucial part, the one thing the judges would look at first. She had titled the bottom axis "bounce height" and the side axis "drop height," and she had felt proud of it until Konnor leaned over from the next table.

"Mine looked like that last night," he said, holding up his own poster, which showed a graph with a small rectangle of white paper pasted over one corner. "I had mine backwards. Arabella caught it at her kitchen table when we were redoing our boards."

Ariana felt her stomach tighten. "Backwards how? It's just two lines with dots on them."

"By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis," Arabella said, arriving with a roll of tape dangling from her wrist. She said it fast, like a line she'd repeated all week. "My brother made me say it ten times."

Ariana stared at her poster. She dropped the ball from heights she chose, one meter, two meters, three meters. Those were her choices, the drops. The bounce height was what came out of the experiment, the thing that depended on what she dropped it from. If that rule was true, she had put each thing on the wrong side. She looked up and down the gymnasium, hunting for evidence, and saw Mr. Pelletier setting up the judges' table near the far doors. She didn't want to ask him and look unprepared, so she walked the rows instead, pretending to stretch her legs, inhaling slowly to calm herself while she peeked at other projects. A plant-growth board had days along the bottom. A music-and-heart-rate board had tempo along the bottom. Every single one put the thing the experimenter chose on the horizontal line.

She hurried back to her table and rummaged through her backpack for graph paper. Konnor slid his pencil box across without being asked. She redrew the whole graph, drop heights marching along the bottom, bounce heights climbing the side, and taped the new sheet over the old one just as Mr. Pelletier called, "Fifteen minutes, people."

The first judge stopped at her table, ran a finger along the fresh graph, and said, "Nice, clean axes. Walk me through it."

"Every drop height I chose runs along here," Ariana said, tapping the bottom of the page, "and the bounce it produced climbs up here."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Losing about 2 percent of body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce athletic performance, especially in endurance events.
story:
Addison stood on the blocks in lane four, squeezed the excess water from her suit, and told herself the tryout was simple: three heats of two hundred metres, and the top four swimmers made the team. She had left her water bottle on the kitchen counter that morning, and when she reached into her bag between warm-up and the first heat, her hand closed on nothing but a damp towel. Alanna leaned over the rope from lane five.

"You can share mine," Alanna said, holding up a squeeze bottle with a shark sticker on it. "It's mostly full."

"Thanks. After heat two," Addison said, because her stomach felt tight when she drank right before racing. She won the first heat easily. Coach circled her time on the clipboard and wrote "exceptional" beside it with a short pencil.

By the middle of the second heat her arms felt heavy, as though someone had slipped weights inside her suit, and her split times crept up even though she was trying harder. She dragged herself out, breathing hard, and found a message on her phone from Alanna, sent from the bench where she was resting between events: "My sister's a sports-science major and she says swimmers sweat more than they think, even in the water. Losing about 2 percent of your body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce performance, especially in endurance events. DRINK. NOW." Addison read it twice. Nobody had said a word about sweat; the pool kept everyone wet and cool, so it was invisible, like a thermostat set too low in a house where you could not see the dial. But the numbers fit. Her body weight was roughly fifty kilos, and two percent of that was about a kilogram, and she had been in the water for over an hour with nothing to drink. She took Alanna's bottle, drank until her throat stopped feeling like a dried sponge, and then drank a little more.

The third heat was the one that counted. Addison pushed off the blocks, and somewhere around the third turn, instead of fading the way she had before, she found her rhythm again. Her arms turned over smoothly, and when she touched the wall, the scoreboard showed her fastest time of the day. Coach wrote her name on the top line of the team list.

On the bus home, Alanna flopped into the seat beside her. "So are you going to carry two bottles from now on, in case you abandon one again?"

"Three bottles," Addison said. She pressed the cold metal of Alanna's shark bottle against her forehead and grinned. "One for me, one for you, and one for whoever forgets theirs."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting: one dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius, two is medium, about 150, and three is high, about 200.
story:
Paige stood in Ms. He's garage, which had been turned into a laundry room with two folding tables and a web of drying lines strung overhead like a canopy. Ms. He had left a note pinned to the washer before driving to the airport, and Paige read it again. "Sort darks from lights, wash cold, and whatever you do, iron the yellow shirt last. Trust me. Ms. He." That last line bothered her all afternoon, because Ms. He never wrote anything without a reason, and Paige was the one who had promised to handle the costumes before the school play on Saturday.

She sorted the pile: towels in one basket, Ewan's black drama T-shirts in another, and the yellow nylon costume shirt alone on the table. When she asked Ewan to help, he admitted his real motive right away. "I only came over because I melted my own shirt at home last year," he said, "and if the same thing happens here, I won't be the only one who ruined something." His grin was infectious, but Paige didn't laugh. The whole class would be watching her walk onstage in that shirt.

She ironed the towels first, on high, which worked fine. Then, without thinking, she laid the yellow shirt flat and ran the iron across the shoulder. A shiny, glazed stripe appeared instantly, smooth as tape. Ewan groaned. "That's the exact thing that happened to mine." Paige set the iron down and turned the shirt over, hunting the label. There it was, a tiny iron symbol with a single dot inside.

"One dot," she said slowly. "The towels had labels with three dots, and they took the high setting." She flipped Ewan's ruined-at-home shirt, which he'd brought in his backpack as evidence, and found two dots on its tag. "So the dots tell you the setting. One dot is low, around 110 degrees. Two is medium, around 150. Three is high, near 200." She turned the iron's dial to low, tested it on a hidden seam of the yellow shirt, and the fabric stayed dull and soft.

They worked out a rescue plan together. Ewan held the shirt taut while Paige laid a damp towel over the shiny stripe and pressed gently through it, careful to keep the dial at one dot. The glare faded, mostly. It would pass from the third row of the audience, which was where their classmates actually sat, because everyone knew the front rows stayed empty.

When she finished, Paige folded the shirt along its seams the way Ms. He's note had diagrammed on the back, wrote "one dot only" on a sticky label, and pressed it inside the collar where the next person would find it. Then she hung it from the drying-line canopy and texted Ms. He a photo. The reply came back in a minute: "Told you to iron it last for a reason."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Demand for necessities, such as essential medicines, changes little when their price changes; economists call this inelastic demand.
story:
The farmers' market smelled like peaches and hot bread, but Zack walked past all of it with five dollars in his fist and one goal: the last basket of blueberries at Mr. Leblanc's stall. Last week those berries had been three dollars, and the week before that, two. Now a hand-written sign read five dollars, and a line of six people stood in front of him.

"Every basket I brought sold out by ten o'clock," Mr. Leblanc was telling a woman at the front. "Frost took half my crop, so this is all there is." The woman paid anyway. So did the man behind her, and the one after that, even when Mr. Leblanc said, "Sorry, gone up again," and crossed out the five and wrote six. Zack watched the basket shrink to the final few pints, and his stomach dropped. At the peach stall next door, piled high with more fruit than anyone was buying, a sign read two dollars, down from four. Nobody rushed. Nobody lined up.

Zack found his friend Laurent sitting on a hay bale, eating a peach. "You're going to inhale that whole thing, pit and all," Zack said, and Laurent laughed and slowed down. Zack sat beside him and frowned at the crowd still gathered around Mr. Leblanc. "It doesn't make sense. He keeps raising the price and they keep buying. Six dollars a pint now. For berries."

"Maybe they'll stop at ten dollars," Laurent offered.

"They won't. My grandma pays whatever it costs for her berry syrup, because she needs it for her stomach. My mom's the same with Grandpa's heart pills at the pharmacy. The pharmacist said the price went up twice this year and everyone still buys them." Zack stood and paced in a small circle, agile enough to dodge a toddler chasing a pigeon. "The peaches are different. Plenty of peaches, so the price drops until people want them. But berries are scarce, and the people who need them, or the medicine people need, they buy it no matter what. It barely changes."

Seamus strolled over with his cousin, who was arguing about a school project on courtroom trials. "I got to be the defendant," the cousin said, "and Seamus wouldn't stop objecting." Seamus grinned, then noticed Zack staring at the blueberry line. "What?"

"Watch," Zack said. He walked back to Mr. Leblanc's stall just in time to hear him say to the last customer, "Eight dollars, and that's the final pint." The customer counted out the bills without a single complaint.

Laurent appeared at Zack's elbow, peach juice still on his chin. "You were right," he whispered.

Zack unfolded his five-dollar bill and looked at it, then at the empty berry baskets stacked behind the stall. "Mr. Leblanc," he called, "got any rhubarb?"

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish generally uses "ser" for lasting traits and "estar" for temporary states: "Mi hermano es alto" means he is tall, while "Mi hermano está cansado" means he is tired.
story:
The market in Cuenca smelled of oranges and fried plantains, and Aaron clutched his notebook like it was a winning lottery ticket. His family had been in Ecuador for five days, and every morning he wrote sentences in Spanish to practice before his teacher, Mr. Owusu, expected a whole recorded presentation when he got home. His brother Marco, who was seventeen and annoying, kept leaning over his shoulder at breakfast to "help."

"Mi hermano está cansado," Aaron read aloud to Adem and Crystal, the twins from the apartment downstairs, who had invited him to the market because their mother sold woven scarves there. Crystal was stacking bracelets, and Adem was attempting to juggle three limes with limited success.

"Wait," Crystal said, squinting at his notebook. "You wrote that sentence with es. Es cansado. My mom says that means he is tired all the time. Like, forever."

Aaron stared at the page. He thought about all the sentences he'd copied: es alto, es cansado, es feliz. The twins' mother waved them over and, between customers, sorted wool with quick fingers. Aaron watched her say "está nublado" about the sky and "es azul" about the wool, and a pattern began to form in his head. He circled every es and every está in his notebook like a detective marking clues. Tall, blue, and happy came with es. Cloudy, tired, and busy came with está.

He tested his idea on Adem. "Tu mamá es amable," he said, pointing at the scarf stall, "y hoy está ocupada." Adem stopped juggling and clapped once. "Sí! That's it. Es for things that stay, está for right now." Aaron grinned and flipped to the sentence about Marco, the one that had started everything. He crossed out the wrong word and wrote the other one above it.

That afternoon, when Marco flopped onto the couch and demanded water, Aaron marched over and recited the corrected sentence. "Mi hermano está cansado. Only today. Not forever." Marco groaned and threw a pillow at him, but their mother laughed so hard she had to sit down, and she let Aaron have the last empanada even though Marco had called dibs.

On the walk home from dinner, Aaron recorded his presentation on his phone, describing his whole family in careful sentences: his mother's curly hair, his father's terrible singing, the dog that was small and white and, today, extremely muddy. When they passed a bakery still glowing at nine o'clock, he bought three rolls with the coins in his pocket and handed one to each of his parents, saving the warmest for Marco, who muttered, "Gracias, hermanito," and split it in half anyway.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, starting the Second World War in Europe, after Hitler demanded the return of Danzig and the Polish Corridor that Germany had lost at Versailles.
story:
Benjamin had three days to figure out one question for Mr. Dela Cruz's class: how did the Treaty of Versailles help lead to the Second World War? Mr. Dela Cruz, whose eccentric habits included pacing the room with a rolled-up map under his arm like a sword, refused to give answers. "You have the library, you have each other," he had said, tapping the question on the whiteboard. "Make me believe it."

At lunch, Benjamin spread his notes across the table in the library corner. Sierra leaned over them, and Lamar dropped his tray down beside hers. Immediately they started arguing about who would do the map and who would write the script for their presentation, so Benjamin mediated, splitting the jobs down the middle before they got loud enough for the librarian's motion sensor to flip the lights off on all of them. Then he pulled the encyclopedia volume toward him and started hunting through 1919.

"Here it is," Sierra said, running her finger down the page. "Versailles. Germany lost land, money, colonies, everything." She flipped to the map and traced a thin strip running to the sea. "Look at this. After the treaty, Germany got cut in two. This bit right here, they call it the Polish Corridor." And at the edge of it sat a city labeled Danzig.

Benjamin copied the shape of the strip onto his own paper, then drew the border from 1914 beside it. Something clicked. Twenty years sat between that map and the war he'd read about last week, and he suddenly needed to know what happened in between. He paged forward, skimming, while Lamar peered over his shoulder. "You look like you found treasure," Lamar said.

"I think I found the bridge," Benjamin said. "Watch." He set two photocopies side by side, the 1919 map and the timeline. "Hitler demanded the return of Danzig and the Polish Corridor. That's the exact land Germany lost at Versailles. And then Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, starting the Second World War in Europe." He tapped the strip on the map, then the date on the timeline. "Versailles didn't start the war. But it's where those places got taken away, and the demand for them back is where it all caught fire."

Sierra grabbed a marker and drew an arrow from the corridor to the date, then circled Danzig in red. "So we start the presentation with this little strip of land," she said, "and we end it with tanks crossing a border."

"Nobody's going to guess it was coming," Lamar said.

"That's the whole point," Benjamin said, and he was already writing their opening line: first, a map that looks boring, and then, twenty years later, a war. He slid the paper across the table so Sierra could make the letters big.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Shaking a baby can cause serious brain injury, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head.
story:
Audrey had assumed babysitting meant pizza, television, and a kid who could at least say what was wrong. What she got instead was six-month-old Milo, who had been screaming for forty straight minutes in Mr. Pierre's living room while his parents were at a retirement dinner for a colleague two streets over.

On the fridge, held up by a magnet shaped like a croissant, hung a note in looping handwriting. Keep bottles in the fridge, warm 20 seconds, and no matter how frustrated you get, NEVER shake him. An infant's neck muscles are too weak to support his heavy head, and shaking can cause serious brain injury. If you're overwhelmed, put him safely in his crib and step away for a minute. Audrey read it twice. The word "frustrated" being right there in a stranger's handwriting, like it was expected of her, was somehow the most insulting part of the evening.

The bottle hadn't worked. The diaper was dry. She had walked him in circles until her arms burned, sung three songs she normally pretended to be indifferent to, and bounced him on her knee until she understood why professional athletes retire young. Milo screamed through all of it, his face a furious red, his fists like tiny detonators. Audrey felt something hot climb up her own neck, and that scared her more than the crying did. So she did what the note said. She laid him in the crib on his back, checked the blanket was nowhere near his face, and walked into the kitchen, where she stood with her hands flat on the counter and counted the tiles.

From the doorway, she watched him and thought. He'd eaten. He was dry. He wasn't sick; his dad had said so. So what was left? She turned the problem over the way she turned over a math proof. A baby this age, she remembered her cousin saying, hasn't yet developed the adaptation of tuning out noise; everything came in at full volume. Audrey glanced at the kitchen light she'd left blazing and the radio murmuring on the counter, both going the whole time because she'd wanted the apartment to feel friendly.

She went back and switched off the lamp and the radio, until the room held only the gray hush from the window. Then she sat in the rocking chair where she could see the crib and stayed very still. The screaming thinned to grumbling, then to hiccupy breathing, then to nothing but the radiator ticking. Milo lay with his eyes open, watching the ceiling like it was the most interesting thing he'd ever seen.

When Mr. Pierre and his wife came home at ten, they found Milo asleep and Audrey doing homework by phone light. "He cried a lot," she said, "and then he didn't." Mr. Pierre counted out her pay and added two extra dollars. "What was it?" his wife whispered. Audrey shrugged and pocketed the money. "Turns out he just wanted everyone to be quiet, including me."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: VisiCalc, written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston and released for the Apple II in 1979, was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers.
story:
Joseph had promised the chess club he would figure out exactly how many games each member had won this season, and Coach Reyes kept the results in a shoebox of crumpled score sheets. The club tournament was in three days, and Eugene wanted a poster with real numbers, not guesses. "If we hand in another poster with smudged tally marks," Eugene said, dropping the box on the library table, "Madeleine will never let us hear the end of it."

Mr. Do, who ran the computer lab after school, handed Joseph a laminated sheet of instructions. "Type your wins in column B," he said, "then ask the machine to add them." Joseph typed names into column A and numbers into column B, all thirty-two rows of them. When he tried to add them by hand on scrap paper, his total came out different twice, and he realized he had skipped a row. He decided the program should comply with his instructions exactly, which meant he had to give it exactly the right ones. In the empty cell below his numbers he typed the formula, and the total appeared, instantly, like something had been waiting under the lid of the box.

The bar chart was harder. His first attempt made one enormous bar and eleven skinny ones, and Joseph stared at it until he understood what was wrong: he had included the total row in the chart's range, so the total towered over everything like a giant at a party. He highlighted the rows again without the total, and the chart snapped into shape. Madeleine leaned over his shoulder. "I want the dynasty bar to be red," she said, pointing at the tallest one, which belonged to her. "I've won four years running, since sixth grade."

At home that night Joseph emailed his grandfather, who used to keep accounts for a small hardware store. The reply came the next morning, and Joseph read it at the lab before school:

Dear Joseph, Your chart reminds me of 1979, when I first saw a spreadsheet on a home computer. It was called VisiCalc, written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston, and it ran on the Apple II, the first spreadsheet program for personal computers. I remember typing in a column of figures and watching the total change when I fixed one number, and thinking I would never add a long column by hand again. Sometimes I miss doing the sums myself, pencil on paper, because I could see every step. Sometimes I don't miss it at all. I'm still not sure which feeling is the honest one. Love, Grandpa.

Joseph read the letter twice, then tried what his grandfather described. He changed one win from a 3 to a 4, and the total at the bottom shifted on its own. So that was the crucial trick, he thought, the reason Mr. Do kept saying formulas were better than typing totals by hand: the total wasn't a number you wrote, it was a rule the machine followed. He imagined his grandfather in 1979 watching the same thing happen on a machine the size of a toaster, and wondered whether the old spreadsheet had felt like magic or like cheating.

He printed the chart with Madeleine's dynasty bar in red, and carried the poster to the gym, where Eugene was already taping up the bracket. "Check the total," Joseph said, tapping the bottom of the page. "It added itself."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: Scientists estimate the Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago.
story:
Alexis stared at the postcard on his grandpa's kitchen table, the Grand Canyon glowing orange under a desert sky. Tomorrow he had to explain in science class how a river could carve a canyon that enormous, and his notecard said only one thing he trusted: scientists estimate the Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago. "That's it?" he groaned. "That's my whole presentation?"

"Use the sink," his grandpa said, not looking up from his crossword.

"The sink?"

"Water moves dirt. Watch it move dirt."

So Alexis filled a baking pan with packed soil from the garden, tilted it over the sink, and turned the faucet to a trickle. At first nothing happened. He sat back, feeling pessimistic about the whole plan, and nearly quit. Then a thin brown line appeared where the water slid across the soil. He let the trickle run. The line deepened into a groove, and tiny crumbs of dirt piled up at the pan's low edge, a small muddy delta.

"Erosion," Alexis said out loud, "and that pile is deposition." The water hadn't smashed the soil apart; it had carried it away, grain by grain, and dropped it wherever the current slowed.

Zaiden's text arrived just then. Presentation canceled? the message asked. No such luck, Alexis typed back. Found something better.

He timed one minute on the kitchen clock and measured the groove with a ruler. Two millimeters. He did the math twice on a napkin because the first answer seemed impossible. Even a tiny stream, if it never stopped, could dig down astonishingly far over years, and the real river had been at it for those 5 to 6 million years. His little pan was a model, a small honest version of an enormous patient thing.

"You look like your grandmother when she was onto something," his grandpa said, finally setting down his pen. He slid his chair over and squinted at the muddy delta. Then he did something Alexis hadn't expected: he plucked the postcard off the table and turned it over. "Your grandma bought this the summer I guided rafts on the Colorado. Never told you that, did I." He hadn't. Grandpa had never disclosed a single story about being a river guide.

"You steered a boat through that?"

"Twice a week, all summer."

Alexis held up the pan. "Then you already knew the river built all this."

Grandpa tapped the muddy delta with one finger. "Five to six million years, the sign at the rim used to say. Your little ditch here, though, that's brand new."

Alexis grinned and turned the faucet back on.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish adjectives usually come after the noun they describe, so "a black cat" is "un gato negro."
story:
The market in Cuenca smelled of oranges and wet stone, and Charlotte's mother had already wandered off toward the fabric stalls. That left Charlotte standing in front of a crate of guinea pigs with an old woman who kept saying something to her in Spanish, slowly, the way people talk to a lost dog. Charlotte knew one thing for certain: she had promised to send her class a video describing her family, in full Spanish sentences, by Friday, and so far she had only learned the words for "hello" and "thank you," which would make a very short video.

"Tengo un gato negro," she said to the guinea pigs, practicing. The old woman smiled, so Charlotte tried the sentence again, this time pointing at a black cat dozing on a stack of grain sacks behind the crate. "Un gato negro." The old woman laughed and said it back to her, and it sounded exactly the same, which was either very good or very bad.

Charlotte found Michaela and Anis by the fountain, where they were meticulously arranging their souvenir coins in rows by size. "I think I said it right," Charlotte said, "but I can't tell. She laughed, but she also pointed at the cat, so maybe I accidentally said something about her grandmother." Anis, who had taken exactly two weeks of Spanish before the trip, squinted at her notebook. "You said gato before negro," he said. "In English we'd say black cat. You said cat black."

They tested it. Michaela invented a sentence on the spot, "una casa blanca," and marched up to a fruit seller to point at a white house across the plaza and say it. He nodded. Then she flipped the words, "una blanca casa," and pointed at the same house. This time the man tilted his head, frowned, and looked around, as if a white house might be hiding somewhere behind the bananas. Charlotte exhaled. It wasn't random, then. The noun came first, and the describing word came after it, the opposite of English, every single time. They tried it with a red apple, a small dog, a tall tower, and the pattern held, a perfect one-to-one ratio of nods to right answers.

Back at the hotel, Charlotte filmed her video on her mother's phone, feeling the words line up backwards and somehow land right. "Tengo una hermana pequeña," she said, and then, because Anis was making faces behind the camera, "tengo un amigo ridículo." Behind her, in the doorway, Mr. O'Brien from the room next door raised his coffee cup and said, "Muy bien."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: All 50 U.S. states, and Washington, D.C., have passed laws on handling concussions in youth sports.
story:
The pool's plumbing hummed under the deck, a low rumble Leah had never noticed until tonight, when everything else had gone quiet. Twelve girls stood along the edge, waiting for Coach to call the next heat. Leah tightened her goggles and glanced at the lane beside hers, where Wali was shaking out her arms the way she always did before a race.

"Fastest two in each heat make the travel squad," Coach said. "Take your marks."

The whistle blew. Leah dove clean, but she heard a splash behind her that was all wrong, a flat smack instead of a cut. When she turned at the wall, she saw Wali in the water near the blocks, holding her head. Wali had slipped on the takeoff and come down hard on the surface, and now the coach was already pulling her out. Leah finished the heat second, but she barely registered it. She climbed out and watched Coach hold up two fingers in front of Wali's face, then move them slowly to one side. Wali tracked them. She said something Leah couldn't hear, and Coach shook her head anyway.

"That's not fair," Leah said to Aydin, who had made the travel squad in the first heat. "Wali looked fine. She followed the fingers. Why pull her?"

"Maybe because she winced when she turned her neck," Aydin said.

Leah couldn't stop thinking about it while she swam her second heat. Wali wasn't dizzy. Wali wasn't confused. So there had to be some other reason, some rule Leah couldn't see, because a coach doesn't pull a girl from her one shot at the team without one. She touched the wall, looked over at the bleachers, and saw Wali sitting with an ice pack, arguing quietly with Ms. McKenzie, the gym teacher who supervised tryouts.

Leah walked over, dripping. "She's fine," Leah said. "You can't just take her out."

"You think I want to?" Ms. McKenzie said. "It's not my choice, or the coach's. Every state in the country, all fifty, plus Washington, D.C., has passed laws about handling concussions in youth sports. A hard hit to the head, the athlete comes out, no exceptions."

Wali stared at her. "There's a law?"

"There's a law."

Leah stood there while the meaning settled over her. It wasn't the coach being cautious, and it wasn't about this pool, or this school, or tonight. The rule was bigger than all of them, and it had been sitting there the whole time, invisible, waiting for exactly this kind of fall.

"Can she try out again next week?" Leah asked.

"If the doctor clears her," Ms. McKenzie said.

Wali looked at Leah and managed a crooked smile. "Save me a spot on that squad."

Leah squeezed the water from her ponytail. "It's saved."
